name: JavaScript
description: A lightweight, interpreted programming language with first-class functions, known as the scripting language for Web pages.

topics.title: JavaScript Fundamentals
topics.content:
1. JavaScript Engine & Runtime

JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted language. The Engine (e.g., V8 in Chrome) parses code, converts it to an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), and compiles it to machine code via a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler. The Runtime includes the engine, Web APIs (DOM, setTimeout), the Callback Queue, and the Event Loop.

2. Variables (var, let, const)

  • var: Function-scoped, hoisted and initialized with undefined.
  • let: Block-scoped, hoisted but kept in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Can be reassigned.
  • const: Block-scoped, hoisted but kept in TDZ. Cannot be reassigned.

// Example
console.log(a); // undefined
var a = 5;

// console.log(b); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 10;

3. Data Types & Equality

Primitives: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint. Reference types: Objects, Arrays, Functions.

== (Loose Equality) performs type coercion. === (Strict Equality) does not.


console.log(5 == "5"); // true
console.log(5 === "5"); // false
console.log(typeof null); // "object" (historic bug)

questions.text: What is the result of `typeof null` in JavaScript?
questions.correctAnswer: object
questions.explanation: Due to a legacy bug in JavaScript, typeof null returns 'object'.

questions.text: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.correctAnswer: let
questions.explanation: let is block-scoped and allows reassignment, unlike const.

questions.text: What is the output of `[] == ![]`?
questions.correctAnswer: true
questions.explanation: ![] evaluates to false. [] == false coerces [] to an empty string '', and false to 0. '' == 0 coerces to 0 == 0, which is true.

questions.text: Which of the following describes the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
options: A time where var declarations are paused
The period between a let/const declaration and its initialization
When the event loop is blocked
questions.correctAnswer: The period between a let/const declaration and its initialization
questions.explanation: Variables declared with let and const exist in the TDZ from the start of the block until the declaration is processed.

questions.text: What does a JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler do in the V8 engine?
options: Compiles code to binary on a server
Compiles code during execution for optimization
questions.correctAnswer: Compiles code during execution for optimization
questions.explanation: JIT compilation combines interpretation and compilation, translating code into machine code during execution and optimizing hot paths.

questions.text: What is the output of `console.log(1 < 2 < 3)` and `console.log(3 > 2 > 1)`?
questions.correctAnswer: true, false
questions.explanation: 1 < 2 evaluates to true. true < 3 coerces true to 1, so 1 < 3 is true. 3 > 2 evaluates to true. true > 1 coerces true to 1, so 1 > 1 is false.

topics.title: Scope & Execution
topics.content:
1. Lexical Scope & Scope Chain

JavaScript uses Lexical Scoping, meaning variable scope is determined by where variables and blocks are physically written in the code. When a variable isn't found in the current scope, the engine looks up the Scope Chain to the parent scope, all the way to the Global Scope.

2. Execution Context

Everything in JS runs inside an Execution Context. The Global Execution Context is created by default. A Function Execution Context is created when a function is invoked.

Phase 1: Memory Creation Phase (Hoisting) - Variables and functions are allocated in memory.

Phase 2: Code Execution Phase - Code is executed line by line.

3. Call Stack

The Call Stack manages Execution Contexts using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) structure. The currently executing function is always at the top of the stack.


function first() {
  second();
  console.log("First");
}
function second() {
  console.log("Second");
}
first(); 
// Output: "Second", then "First"
// Stack trace: Global -> first() -> second() -> pop second() -> pop first()

questions.text: What is Lexical Scoping?
options: Scope determined by the function caller at runtime
Scope determined by where variables are declared in the source code
Scope that is restricted to the browser window
Scope determined by the this keyword
questions.correctAnswer: Scope determined by where variables are declared in the source code
questions.explanation: Lexical scope means scope is defined at lexing time (compile time) based on where things are physically written.

questions.text: What data structure does the JavaScript engine use to keep track of function execution?
questions.correctAnswer: Stack
questions.explanation: The Call Stack uses a LIFO (Last In, First Out) structure to manage execution contexts.

questions.text: During the Memory Creation Phase of an Execution Context, what value is assigned to `var` declarations?
options: The assigned value in the code
questions.correctAnswer: undefined
questions.explanation: Variables declared with var are hoisted and initially set to undefined during the creation phase.

questions.text: What happens when a variable is not found in the current scope?
options: The engine looks down the scope chain to child scopes
The engine looks up the scope chain to parent scopes
The variable is automatically created in the current scope
questions.correctAnswer: The engine looks up the scope chain to parent scopes
questions.explanation: The scope chain defines how variables are resolved. It travels upwards from inner scopes to outer scopes.

questions.text: What is Variable Shadowing?
options: When a variable is hidden by the TDZ
When an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer scope variable
When a variable is garbage collected
questions.correctAnswer: When an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer scope variable
questions.explanation: Shadowing occurs when a local variable shares the same name as a variable in the outer scope, effectively 'hiding' the outer variable.

questions.text: What happens if the Call Stack exceeds its maximum size?
options: A RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded is thrown
The browser allocates more memory automatically
questions.correctAnswer: A RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded is thrown
questions.explanation: This is known as a stack overflow, typically caused by infinite recursion, resulting in a RangeError.

topics.title: Functions & Closures
topics.content:
1. Higher-Order Functions

Functions in JS are first-class citizens, meaning they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. A Higher-Order Function is a function that takes a function as an argument or returns one.

2. Pure Functions

A pure function always produces the same output for the same input and produces no side effects (e.g., modifying global state or DOM).

3. Closures

A Closure is a function that remembers its outer variables and can access them even after the outer function has finished executing. The inner function preserves the lexical scope of the outer function.


// Closure for Data Privacy
function createCounter() {
  let count = 0; // Private variable
  return function() {
    count++;
    return count;
  }
}
const counter = createCounter();
console.log(counter()); // 1
console.log(counter()); // 2

questions.text: What is a Higher-Order Function?
options: A function that executes very fast
A function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function
A function declared inside an object
questions.correctAnswer: A function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function
questions.explanation: Because functions are first-class citizens in JS, they can be treated like any other variable, allowing higher-order functions.

questions.text: What is a Closure?
options: A function that is immediately invoked
A function bundled with its lexical environment
A function that has no side effects
questions.correctAnswer: A function bundled with its lexical environment
questions.explanation: A closure allows an inner function to access an outer function's scope even after the outer function has returned.

questions.text: What is the primary benefit of using closures in JavaScript?
options: They allow for data privacy and encapsulation
They prevent the Event Loop from blocking
They act as a substitute for Promises
questions.correctAnswer: They allow for data privacy and encapsulation
questions.explanation: Closures allow you to create private variables that cannot be accessed or modified directly from the outside.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)?
questions.correctAnswer: (function() { })()
questions.explanation: An IIFE is defined inside parentheses to make it an expression, followed by () to invoke it immediately.

questions.text: What is Function Currying?
options: Translating a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of nested functions each taking a single argument
Caching the results of a function
questions.correctAnswer: Translating a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of nested functions each taking a single argument
questions.explanation: Currying transforms a function like f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c).

questions.text: What is the output of this closure loop? `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }`
questions.explanation: Because `var` is function scoped, there is only one `i` binding. The loop finishes synchronously making `i = 3` before any of the asynchronous setTimeouts run.

topics.title: Objects
topics.content:
1. Object Creation & Properties

Objects are collections of key-value pairs. Keys are strings (or Symbols). Values can be any data type. You can create objects using object literals {}, the new Object() syntax, or Object.create().

2. Object Methods

  • Object.keys(obj): Returns an array of keys.
  • Object.values(obj): Returns an array of values.
  • Object.entries(obj): Returns an array of [key, value] pairs.
  • Object.assign(target, source): Copies properties from source to target.

3. Immutability

Object.freeze() makes an object entirely immutable. Object.seal() prevents adding or removing properties, but allows modifying existing ones.


const user = { name: "Alice", role: "Admin" };
Object.freeze(user);
user.name = "Bob"; // Fails silently in non-strict mode
console.log(user.name); // "Alice"

4. Shallow vs Deep Copy

The spread operator {...obj} creates a shallow copy. Nested objects are still referenced by memory address. To create a deep copy, you can use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) or the modern structuredClone(obj).

questions.text: What is the result of using the spread operator `{...obj}` on an object with nested objects?
options: A complete deep clone is created
A shallow copy is created; nested objects share the same memory reference
The nested objects are converted to strings
questions.correctAnswer: A shallow copy is created; nested objects share the same memory reference
questions.explanation: The spread operator only copies the first level of properties. Nested objects copy by reference.

questions.text: Which method returns an array of a given object's own enumerable string-keyed property [key, value] pairs?
questions.correctAnswer: Object.entries()
questions.explanation: Object.entries() returns an array containing arrays of the [key, value] pairs.

questions.text: What is the difference between Object.freeze() and Object.seal()?
options: freeze allows modifying existing properties, seal does not
seal allows modifying existing properties, freeze does not
freeze is for arrays, seal is for objects
questions.correctAnswer: seal allows modifying existing properties, freeze does not
questions.explanation: Object.seal() prevents adding/removing properties but allows changing existing ones. freeze() makes the object completely immutable.

questions.text: How does the modern `structuredClone()` function improve upon `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())`?
options: It works in older browsers natively
It can clone Maps, Sets, Dates, and handle circular references
questions.correctAnswer: It can clone Maps, Sets, Dates, and handle circular references
questions.explanation: structuredClone is the modern native way to deep clone objects and supports complex types that JSON stringification breaks on.

questions.text: What happens when you try to reassign a property of an Object.freeze() object in Strict Mode?
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a TypeError
questions.explanation: In non-strict mode it fails silently, but in strict mode, mutating a frozen object throws a TypeError.

questions.text: If obj = { a: 1 }, what does Object.defineProperty(obj, 'b', { value: 2 }) do if 'enumerable' is not specified?
options: Creates 'b', which shows up in Object.keys()
Creates 'b', but it does NOT show up in Object.keys()
questions.correctAnswer: Creates 'b', but it does NOT show up in Object.keys()
questions.explanation: By default, properties added via Object.defineProperty are not enumerable, not configurable, and not writable unless explicitly set to true.

topics.title: Prototypes & Inheritance
topics.content:
1. The Prototype Chain

Every object in JavaScript has a built-in property called its prototype. The prototype is itself an object, so the prototype will have its own prototype, making a prototype chain. The chain ends when it reaches a prototype that has null for its own prototype.

2. __proto__ vs prototype

__proto__ is the actual object that is used in the lookup chain to resolve methods, etc. prototype is the object that is used to build __proto__ when you create an object with new.

3. ES6 Classes

Classes in JS are syntactic sugar over the existing prototype-based inheritance. They provide a cleaner syntax to create objects and deal with inheritance.


class Animal {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  speak() {
    console.log(this.name + ' makes a noise.');
  }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name); // Call the parent constructor
  }
  speak() {
    console.log(this.name + ' barks.');
  }
}

questions.text: What keyword is used to inherit from a parent class in ES6?
questions.correctAnswer: extends
questions.explanation: The 'extends' keyword is used in class declarations or class expressions to create a class that is a child of another class.

questions.text: What is the top-most prototype in the JavaScript prototype chain?
questions.correctAnswer: Object.prototype
questions.explanation: Nearly all objects in JavaScript are instances of Object; a typical object inherits properties from Object.prototype.

questions.text: What does the `super()` function do in a child class constructor?
questions.correctAnswer: Calls the parent class's constructor
questions.explanation: In a derived class with a constructor, you must call super() before you can use 'this'.

questions.text: How can you programmatically get the prototype of a specific object instance?
questions.correctAnswer: Object.getPrototypeOf(object)
questions.explanation: Object.getPrototypeOf() is the standard method to get the prototype of an object, rather than using the deprecated __proto__ property.

questions.text: What is the difference between an object's `__proto__` and a function's `prototype` property?
options: __proto__ is the actual prototype chain link for an instance; prototype is the object attached to instances created via 'new' on that function
prototype is for arrays, __proto__ is for objects
__proto__ is a method, prototype is a string
questions.correctAnswer: __proto__ is the actual prototype chain link for an instance; prototype is the object attached to instances created via 'new' on that function
questions.explanation: The 'prototype' property on a constructor function is what it *assigns* to the __proto__ of instances it creates.

questions.text: What happens if you define a method inside an ES6 class without the `static` keyword?
options: It is attached to the class itself, not instances
It is attached to the instance's prototype
It is attached directly to the instance object
questions.correctAnswer: It is attached to the instance's prototype
questions.explanation: Standard methods in a class body are placed on the class's prototype, so all instances share the same function reference.

topics.title: `this` Keyword
topics.content:
1. Execution Context Binding

The value of this is evaluated at runtime depending on the function's execution context. It behaves differently in strict mode vs non-strict mode.

2. The 4 Rules of 'this' Binding

  • Implicit Binding: When a function is called as a method of an object (e.g., obj.method()), this points to the object.
  • Explicit Binding: Using .call(), .apply(), or .bind() to explicitly state what this should be.
  • New Binding: When a function is called with the new keyword, this points to the newly created instance.
  • Default Binding: A standalone function invocation defaults this to the global object (window) or undefined in strict mode.

3. Arrow Functions

Arrow functions do not have their own this context. They inherit this lexically from the parent scope at the time they are defined.


const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  regularFunc: function() { console.log(this.name); },
  arrowFunc: () => { console.log(this.name); }
};
user.regularFunc(); // "Alice"
user.arrowFunc(); // undefined (inherits from window)

questions.text: What does `this` refer to in a standard standalone function call in non-strict mode?
options: The Global Object (e.g., window in browsers)
questions.correctAnswer: The Global Object (e.g., window in browsers)
questions.explanation: Default binding points 'this' to the global object when not in strict mode.

questions.text: How do Arrow Functions handle the `this` keyword?
options: They bind it to the object calling them
They bind it to the global object always
They lexically bind it to the enclosing scope
They throw an error if this is used
questions.correctAnswer: They lexically bind it to the enclosing scope
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not bind their own 'this'. They inherit it from the parent scope.

questions.text: What is the difference between `.call()` and `.apply()`?
options: .call takes arguments as an array; .apply takes arguments separated by commas
.apply takes arguments as an array; .call takes arguments separated by commas
.call returns a new function; .apply executes it immediately
questions.correctAnswer: .apply takes arguments as an array; .call takes arguments separated by commas
questions.explanation: Both invoke the function immediately and explicitly set 'this', but apply expects an array of arguments (A for Array).

questions.text: What does `.bind()` return?
options: The result of the function execution
A new function with the `this` context permanently bound
questions.correctAnswer: A new function with the `this` context permanently bound
questions.explanation: .bind() does not execute the function immediately; it returns a new bound instance of the function.

questions.text: What happens if you use the `new` keyword on an arrow function?
options: It creates a new object successfully
It throws a TypeError because arrow functions are not constructors
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a TypeError because arrow functions are not constructors
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not have a [[Construct]] method and cannot be used with 'new'.

questions.text: If `const bound = fn.bind(obj1);`, what happens if you call `bound.call(obj2)`?
questions.correctAnswer: 'this' remains obj1
questions.explanation: Once a function is bound using .bind(), its 'this' context cannot be changed again, even with .call() or .apply().

topics.title: Arrays
topics.content:
1. Array Methods Overview

JavaScript provides numerous built-in methods for array manipulation. Understanding which methods mutate the original array versus returning a new array is critical for React and Functional Programming.

2. Mutating Methods

  • push() / pop(): Add/remove from end.
  • shift() / unshift(): Add/remove from beginning.
  • splice(start, deleteCount, item1...): Modifies array in place.
  • sort() / reverse(): Mutates original array in place.

3. Non-Mutating (Immutable) Methods

  • map(): Returns a new array with transformed elements.
  • filter(): Returns a new array with elements that pass a test.
  • reduce(): Reduces the array to a single value.
  • slice(start, end): Returns a shallow copy of a portion of an array.

const nums = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]
console.log(nums); // [1, 2, 3] (original unchanged)

questions.text: Which array method modifies the original array?
questions.correctAnswer: splice()
questions.explanation: splice() adds/removes items to/from an array, changing the original array.

questions.text: What does the `.map()` method return?
options: A completely new array with the results of calling a provided function on every element
questions.correctAnswer: A completely new array with the results of calling a provided function on every element
questions.explanation: map() is an immutable method that transforms every element and returns a new array.

questions.text: What is the difference between `slice()` and `splice()`?
options: slice mutates the array; splice returns a copy
splice mutates the array; slice returns a copy
questions.correctAnswer: splice mutates the array; slice returns a copy
questions.explanation: slice(start, end) returns a portion of the array without modifying it. splice() modifies the array in place.

questions.text: How does the `.reduce()` method work?
options: It removes elements from an array
It executes a reducer function on each element, resulting in a single output value
It returns an array of booleans
questions.correctAnswer: It executes a reducer function on each element, resulting in a single output value
questions.explanation: reduce() takes an accumulator and the current value, and iterates through the array to produce a single final value.

questions.text: By default, how does the `sort()` method sort elements?
options: It converts elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 code unit values sequences
questions.correctAnswer: It converts elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 code unit values sequences
questions.explanation: Without a compare function, sort() converts elements to strings. This means [1, 10, 2] sorts to [1, 10, 2] instead of [1, 2, 10].

questions.text: What is an 'Array-Like Object' and how can you convert it to a real Array?
options: An object with a .length property; use Array.from()
An object with numeric keys; use JSON.parse()
questions.correctAnswer: An object with a .length property; use Array.from()
questions.explanation: Objects like the `arguments` object or DOM NodeLists have numeric indices and a length property, but lack array methods. Array.from() converts them to real arrays.

topics.title: Strings & Regex
topics.content:
1. String Methods

Strings are immutable primitives. Important methods include split(), slice(), substring(), replace(), trim(), and includes().

2. Template Literals

Introduced in ES6, they use backticks and allow multi-line strings and interpolation using ${expression}.


const name = "World";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

3. Regular Expressions (Regex)

Used for pattern matching. Flags include g (global), i (case-insensitive), and m (multiline).

  • ^ matches the beginning of input.
  • $ matches the end of input.
  • + matches 1 or more times.
  • * matches 0 or more times.

questions.text: Which string method extracts a section of a string and returns it as a new string, without modifying the original string?
questions.correctAnswer: slice()
questions.explanation: slice(start, end) extracts a portion of a string. splice() is an array method, not a string method.

questions.text: What syntax is used for string interpolation in ES6 template literals?
questions.correctAnswer: ${expression}
questions.explanation: Template literals use backticks and ${} to embed expressions.

questions.text: What is the difference between `substring()` and `substr()`?
options: substring takes a start and end index; substr takes a start index and a length
substr takes a start and end index; substring takes a start index and a length
questions.correctAnswer: substring takes a start and end index; substr takes a start index and a length
questions.explanation: Note: substr() is considered legacy and its use should be avoided in modern code.

questions.text: What does the regular expression flag 'i' do?
questions.correctAnswer: Case-insensitive search
questions.explanation: The 'i' flag ignores case when matching letters.

questions.text: In regular expressions, what does a Lookahead `(?=...)` do?
options: Asserts that what immediately follows the current position in the string matches the pattern, without consuming characters
Replaces the pattern with the specified string
questions.correctAnswer: Asserts that what immediately follows the current position in the string matches the pattern, without consuming characters
questions.explanation: Lookaheads are zero-width assertions. They check if a pattern exists ahead without moving the regex pointer.

questions.text: What is the output of `"hello".replace(/l/g, "1")`?
questions.correctAnswer: he11o
questions.explanation: The 'g' flag ensures that all occurrences of 'l' are replaced with '1'.

topics.title: Modern ES6+
topics.content:
1. Destructuring & Spread/Rest

Destructuring allows you to unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables. The Rest operator (...args) collects multiple elements into a single array. The Spread operator expands iterables into individual elements.

2. Optional Chaining (?.) & Nullish Coalescing (??)

Optional chaining allows reading the value of a property located deep within a chain without throwing an error if a reference is nullish.

Nullish Coalescing returns its right-hand side operand when its left-hand side is exactly null or undefined.


const user = { profile: { name: "Alice" } };
console.log(user?.profile?.age ?? 25); // 25

3. Collections (Map, Set)

Map holds key-value pairs and remembers insertion order. Any value can be used as either a key or a value. Set lets you store unique values of any type.

questions.text: What does the Spread operator (`...`) do when used on an array?
options: It condenses the array into a single string
It expands the array elements into individual arguments/elements
questions.correctAnswer: It expands the array elements into individual arguments/elements
questions.explanation: Spread 'unpacks' an iterable. E.g., Math.max(...[1, 2, 3]) becomes Math.max(1, 2, 3).

questions.text: Which modern feature safely accesses deeply nested object properties without throwing a TypeError?
questions.correctAnswer: Optional Chaining
questions.explanation: Optional Chaining (?.) short-circuits and returns undefined if the property before it is null or undefined.

questions.text: How is a Map different from a standard Object?
options: Maps can only have string keys
Maps do not remember insertion order
Maps allow keys of any data type (including objects and functions)
questions.correctAnswer: Maps allow keys of any data type (including objects and functions)
questions.explanation: Unlike regular objects which convert keys to strings/symbols, Maps can use objects, functions, or any primitive as a key.

questions.text: What happens when you add a duplicate value to a `Set`?
options: It creates an array of that value
questions.correctAnswer: It simply ignores the duplicate
questions.explanation: A Set is a collection of unique values. Adding a duplicate has no effect.

questions.text: What is the difference between `||` (Logical OR) and `??` (Nullish Coalescing)?
options: `||` returns the right side if the left is falsey (e.g., 0, ''); `??` only returns the right side if the left is strictly null or undefined
`??` returns the right side if the left is falsey; `||` checks for null/undefined
questions.correctAnswer: `||` returns the right side if the left is falsey (e.g., 0, ''); `??` only returns the right side if the left is strictly null or undefined
questions.explanation: This is crucial when 0 or '' are valid values that shouldn't be overwritten by defaults.

questions.text: What does the Rest operator do in function parameters? E.g., `function foo(a, ...b) {}`
options: It creates a copy of the arguments object
It collects all remaining arguments into an array
It expands an array into individual arguments
questions.correctAnswer: It collects all remaining arguments into an array
questions.explanation: In function definitions, ...b gathers the rest of the comma-separated arguments into a standard array named b.

topics.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
topics.content:
1. The Event Loop

JS is single-threaded. It handles concurrency using the Event Loop. Synchronous code executes first on the Call Stack. Asynchronous callbacks are sent to the Web APIs, then to Queues.

  • Microtask Queue: Promises (.then, catch, finally), queueMicrotask, MutationObserver.
  • Macrotask Queue: setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events, fetch callbacks.

The Event Loop empties the entire Microtask queue before running a single Macrotask.

2. Promises

A Promise represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. It has three states: Pending, Fulfilled, or Rejected.


Promise.resolve(1)
  .then(res => res * 2)
  .then(res => console.log(res)); // 2

3. Async / Await

Syntactic sugar over Promises. An async function always returns a Promise. The await keyword pauses the execution of the async function until the Promise settles.

questions.text: What are the three possible states of a Promise?
questions.correctAnswer: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected
questions.explanation: A Promise starts as Pending, and then settles into either a Fulfilled (success) or Rejected (failure) state.

questions.text: What keyword is used to pause the execution of an async function until a Promise settles?
questions.correctAnswer: await
questions.explanation: The await keyword blocks the execution of code within the async function until the awaited Promise is resolved or rejected.

questions.text: Which queue has a higher priority in the Event Loop?
questions.correctAnswer: Microtask Queue
questions.explanation: After the Call Stack is empty, the Event Loop will process all tasks in the Microtask Queue before moving on to the Macrotask Queue.

questions.text: What happens if a Promise in `Promise.all()` rejects?
options: It waits for the others to finish and returns an array of successes
The entire Promise.all rejects immediately with that error
It ignores the error and continues
questions.correctAnswer: The entire Promise.all rejects immediately with that error
questions.explanation: Promise.all() has fail-fast behavior. If one rejects, the whole thing rejects immediately. Use Promise.allSettled() if you want to wait for all regardless of failure.

questions.text: What does `Promise.race()` do?
options: Returns the first Promise to fulfill, ignoring rejections
Returns the first Promise to settle (either fulfill or reject)
Slows down Promise execution for debugging
questions.correctAnswer: Returns the first Promise to settle (either fulfill or reject)
questions.explanation: Promise.race() resolves or rejects as soon as the *first* promise in the iterable resolves or rejects.

questions.text: What is the output? `setTimeout(()=>console.log('A'),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log('B')); console.log('C');`
questions.correctAnswer: C, B, A
questions.explanation: 'C' is sync (Call Stack). 'B' is a microtask (Promise). 'A' is a macrotask (setTimeout). Order is Stack -> Micro -> Macro.

topics.title: DOM & Browser APIs
topics.content:
1. The DOM (Document Object Model)

The DOM is an object-oriented representation of the web page. We use JS to select elements (querySelector) and modify them.

2. Event Propagation

When an event occurs, it travels through the DOM tree in three phases:

  1. Capturing Phase: Travels down from the window to the target.
  2. Target Phase: Reaches the target element.
  3. Bubbling Phase: Bubbles up from the target back to the window.

Event Delegation is the pattern of attaching a single event listener to a parent element to catch bubbling events from its children.

3. Web Storage

localStorage (persists until deleted, ~5MB) vs sessionStorage (cleared when tab closes).

questions.text: What is the difference between event bubbling and event capturing?
options: Bubbling goes from target to root, capturing goes from root to target
Capturing goes from target to root, bubbling goes from root to target
Capturing stops the event, bubbling does not
questions.correctAnswer: Bubbling goes from target to root, capturing goes from root to target
questions.explanation: Event bubbling propagates upwards. Capturing propagates downwards.

questions.text: Which method prevents an event from propagating further in the capturing and bubbling phases?
questions.correctAnswer: event.stopPropagation()
questions.explanation: stopPropagation() stops the event from moving up or down the DOM tree.

questions.text: What is the storage capacity limit for LocalStorage in most modern browsers?
questions.correctAnswer: ~5MB
questions.explanation: LocalStorage is limited to about 5MB per origin.

questions.text: What does `event.preventDefault()` do?
options: Prevents the default browser action for that event
questions.correctAnswer: Prevents the default browser action for that event
questions.explanation: It stops things like form submissions from reloading the page or links from navigating.

questions.text: What is Event Delegation?
options: Passing events to a Web Worker
Attaching a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from multiple dynamic children
questions.correctAnswer: Attaching a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from multiple dynamic children
questions.explanation: Event delegation leverages event bubbling to handle events efficiently at a higher level, which is great for dynamically added elements.

questions.text: How can you attach an event listener that triggers during the Capturing phase rather than the Bubbling phase?
options: It's not possible in modern browsers
questions.correctAnswer: element.addEventListener('click', fn, true)
questions.explanation: Passing `true` as the third argument to addEventListener (the `useCapture` flag) sets the listener to trigger during the capturing phase.

topics.title: Modules & Memory Management
topics.content:
1. JavaScript Modules

Modules allow splitting code into separate files. ES Modules (ESM) use import / export. CommonJS (CJS) uses require() / module.exports (common in older Node.js).

2. Memory & Garbage Collection

Memory is allocated in the Stack (static data, primitives) and the Heap (objects, arrays). JS automatically clears unused memory using a Garbage Collector.

The most common GC algorithm is Mark-and-Sweep. It starts at the roots (global object) and marks all reachable objects. Unreachable objects are swept away.

3. Memory Leaks

Common causes of memory leaks include accidental global variables, uncleared intervals/timers, and unremoved event listeners holding references to DOM elements.

questions.text: Which syntax is used for importing a module in standard ES Modules (ES6)?
questions.correctAnswer: import { x } from 'module'
questions.explanation: ES Modules use the import and export keywords.

questions.text: Where are primitive values and execution contexts stored in memory?
questions.correctAnswer: The Stack
questions.explanation: The Stack handles static memory allocation (primitives and function calls), while the Heap handles dynamic memory (objects).

questions.text: What is the primary Garbage Collection algorithm used by modern JavaScript engines?
questions.correctAnswer: Mark-and-Sweep
questions.explanation: Mark-and-Sweep finds all reachable objects starting from the global root. Anything unreachable is collected.

questions.text: Which keyword is used in ES Modules to export a single, fallback value from a module?
questions.correctAnswer: export default
questions.explanation: export default allows you to export exactly one default value from a file.

questions.text: What is a common cause of a memory leak in a Single Page Application (SPA)?
options: Failing to call `removeEventListener` when a component unmounts
questions.correctAnswer: Failing to call `removeEventListener` when a component unmounts
questions.explanation: If an event listener references a DOM element or component state and is never removed, it prevents the Garbage Collector from freeing that memory even after the component is gone.

questions.text: Why might you use a `WeakMap` instead of a standard `Map`?
options: WeakMap allows garbage collection of its keys if there are no other references to them
questions.correctAnswer: WeakMap allows garbage collection of its keys if there are no other references to them
questions.explanation: WeakMaps hold 'weak' references to object keys. If the object key is deleted elsewhere, it gets garbage collected from the WeakMap too, preventing memory leaks.

topics.title: Functional Programming & Error Handling
topics.content:
1. Functional Programming Concepts

Pure Functions: No side effects, same input = same output.

Immutability: Data should not be changed after creation. Instead, create new copies.

Currying: Transforming a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions, each taking a single argument.

2. Error Handling

Errors are handled using try...catch...finally blocks. You can create custom errors by extending the Error class.


try {
  throw new Error("Something broke!");
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.message);
} finally {
  console.log("Runs no matter what.");
}

questions.text: What is a Pure Function?
options: A function with no side effects that always returns the same output for the same input
questions.correctAnswer: A function with no side effects that always returns the same output for the same input
questions.explanation: Pure functions do not mutate external state and are highly predictable.

questions.text: What happens in a `finally` block?
options: It only runs if an error occurs
It only runs if no error occurs
It executes regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught
questions.correctAnswer: It executes regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught
questions.explanation: The finally block is used for cleanup code and runs unconditionally after try and catch.

questions.text: What is Currying in JavaScript?
options: Evaluating a function with multiple arguments as a sequence of functions, each taking a single argument
questions.correctAnswer: Evaluating a function with multiple arguments as a sequence of functions, each taking a single argument
questions.explanation: Currying transforms a function f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c).

questions.text: Does a `finally` block execute if a `return` statement is inside the `try` block?
options: Only if an error is thrown
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, always
questions.explanation: The finally block executes even if a return statement is encountered in the try or catch blocks.

questions.text: In Functional Programming, what is 'Referential Transparency'?
options: The ability to access private variables
An expression that can be replaced with its corresponding value without changing the program's behavior
questions.correctAnswer: An expression that can be replaced with its corresponding value without changing the program's behavior
questions.explanation: Referential transparency implies that a function is pure and evaluating it gives the same value for the same arguments every time.

questions.text: How do you correctly handle an error inside an asynchronous `setTimeout` callback using `try...catch`?
options: Wrap the setTimeout call in a try...catch
Wrap the code INSIDE the setTimeout callback in a try...catch
Errors in setTimeout cannot be caught
questions.correctAnswer: Wrap the code INSIDE the setTimeout callback in a try...catch
questions.explanation: A try...catch block is synchronous. By the time the setTimeout callback runs on the Event Loop, the surrounding try...catch has already finished executing. The try...catch must be inside the callback.

topics.title: Generators and Iterators
topics.content:
Generators

Generators are functions that can be exited and later re-entered. Defined using function* and the yield keyword.

questions.text: What does the yield keyword do in a generator function?
options: It permanently stops the function execution
It returns a value and pauses the execution of the generator
questions.correctAnswer: It returns a value and pauses the execution of the generator
questions.explanation: yield pauses the generator function and returns an IteratorResult object to the caller.

topics.title: Memory Management & Garbage Collection
topics.content:
Garbage Collection

JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore. The main algorithm used is Mark-and-Sweep.

questions.text: Which algorithm is primarily used by modern JavaScript engines for garbage collection?
questions.correctAnswer: Mark-and-Sweep
questions.explanation: Modern engines use Mark-and-Sweep.

topics.title: Browser APIs & DOM
topics.content:
The Browser

DOM selection, traversal, manipulation, event bubbling/capturing, delegation, LocalStorage, Fetch API, and Web Workers.

questions.text: What is Event Delegation?
options: Passing events to a web worker
Attaching a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from multiple children
Preventing the default action of an event
questions.correctAnswer: Attaching a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from multiple children
questions.explanation: Event delegation leverages event bubbling to handle events efficiently at a higher level in the DOM tree.

topics.title: Regular Expressions
topics.content:
Regex

Patterns, character classes, quantifiers, groups, lookahead/lookbehind, and flags.

questions.text: What does the 'g' flag do in a Regular Expression?
questions.correctAnswer: Global search (finds all matches)
questions.explanation: The 'g' flag tells the regex engine to search the entire string and return all matches, rather than stopping after the first match.

topics.title: JSON & Data Handling
topics.content:
JSON

JSON.parse(), JSON.stringify(), serialization, circular references, and data transformation.

questions.text: What happens when you call JSON.stringify() on an object containing a circular reference?
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a TypeError
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify() cannot serialize circular structures and will throw a 'Converting circular structure to JSON' TypeError.

topics.title: Security
topics.content:
Security

XSS, CSRF, Prototype Pollution, CSP, Secure Cookies, CORS, and Same-Origin Policy.

questions.text: What does CORS stand for?
questions.correctAnswer: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
questions.explanation: CORS is an HTTP-header based mechanism that allows a server to indicate any origins other than its own from which a browser should permit loading resources.

topics.title: Node.js-Specific JavaScript
topics.content:
Node.js Specifics

V8 Engine, Node Event Loop, Streams, Buffers, global, process, and worker threads.

questions.text: What is the global object equivalent to the browser's `window` in Node.js?
questions.correctAnswer: global
questions.explanation: In Node.js, the top-level scope is not the global scope (due to modules), but the `global` object serves as the global namespace.

topics.title: Interview Coding Topics
topics.content:
Coding Questions

String manipulation, arrays, flattening, deep cloning, grouping, chunking, and recursion.

questions.text: Which array method is best for deeply flattening an array?
questions.correctAnswer: Array.prototype.flat(Infinity)
questions.explanation: Calling flat() with Infinity as the depth parameter will recursively flatten an array of arbitrary depth.

topics.title: Output-Based Interview Questions
topics.content:
Output-Based Questions

Predicting the output of tricky code snippets involving hoisting, scope, closures, Promises, and the event loop.

questions.text: What is the output of: `console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3)`?
questions.correctAnswer: false
questions.explanation: Due to floating point precision in IEEE 754, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly equal to 0.3.

topics.title: Polyfills
topics.content:
Polyfills

A polyfill is a piece of code (usually JavaScript on the Web) used to provide modern functionality on older browsers that do not natively support it.

questions.text: When implementing a custom polyfill for Array.prototype.map, what is the most important rule about the return value?
options: It must return a modified version of the original array
It must return a completely new array
questions.correctAnswer: It must return a completely new array
questions.explanation: The map() method always creates and returns a new array populated with the results.

topics.title: Debouncing and Throttling Implementation
topics.content:
Advanced Optimization

Writing custom debounce and throttle functions is a common interview task to test understanding of closures and setTimeout.

questions.text: In a custom debounce function, what happens if the function is called again before the timeout completes?
options: A second timeout is started in parallel
The previous timeout is cleared and a new one starts
The new call is completely ignored
questions.correctAnswer: The previous timeout is cleared and a new one starts
questions.explanation: Debouncing resets the timer on every call using clearTimeout(timerId) so the function only runs after a period of inactivity.

topics.title: Deep Equality Implementation
topics.content:
Deep Equals

Writing a function to determine if two deeply nested objects or arrays are structurally identical.

questions.text: When writing a deep equality function, what is the edge case when comparing two null values using typeof?
questions.correctAnswer: typeof null is 'object'
questions.explanation: Because typeof null returns 'object', you must explicitly check if the value is null before treating it as a standard object in your deep equality logic.

topics.title: Event Emitter Implementation
topics.content:
Publish/Subscribe Pattern

Implementing a basic Event Emitter (pub/sub) class with 'on', 'emit', and 'off' methods.

questions.text: In a custom Event Emitter, what data structure is best used to store the registered events and their callbacks?
options: An Object (or Map) where keys are event names and values are arrays of functions
questions.correctAnswer: An Object (or Map) where keys are event names and values are arrays of functions
questions.explanation: You need a dictionary to map a specific event name to a list (array) of listener functions that should be executed when emitted.

topics.title: Promise Implementation
topics.content:
Custom Promises

Understanding how a Promise works under the hood by implementing custom resolve, reject, and then chaining mechanisms.

questions.text: When implementing a custom Promise, how do you ensure the '.then' callbacks are executed asynchronously?
options: By wrapping the callback execution in setTimeout or queueMicrotask
questions.correctAnswer: By wrapping the callback execution in setTimeout or queueMicrotask
questions.explanation: According to the Promise A+ spec, 'then' callbacks must not be executed synchronously. They must be deferred to a microtask queue or macro task queue.

topics.title: Hoisting Output Questions
topics.content:
Hoisting in Practice

Predicting the output of variables accessed before declaration.

questions.text: What is the output of: `console.log(a); var a = 5;`?
questions.correctAnswer: undefined
questions.explanation: With `var`, the declaration is hoisted to the top of the scope, but the initialization (= 5) is not.

topics.title: Event Loop Output Questions
topics.content:
Event Loop execution order

Predicting the exact execution order of sync code, Microtasks (Promises), and Macrotasks (setTimeout).

questions.text: What is the output? `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);`
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Then Microtasks like Promises run (3). Finally, Macrotasks like setTimeout run (2).

topics.title: Closure Output Questions
topics.content:
Closures and Loops

Predicting the output of callbacks inside loops referencing `var` vs `let`.

questions.text: What is the output? `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); }`
questions.explanation: `var` is function-scoped. By the time the timeouts run, the loop has finished and `i` is 3. The callbacks all reference the same `i`.

topics.title: This Keyword Output Questions
topics.content:
Context Prediction

Determining what `this` evaluates to inside nested objects and arrow functions.

questions.text: What is the output? `const obj = { name: 'Dev', getName: () => this.name }; console.log(obj.getName());`
questions.correctAnswer: undefined
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not bind their own `this`. They inherit `this` from the enclosing lexical scope (the global object window here), which doesn't have a `name` property.

name: React.js
description: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

topics.title: Virtual DOM & Reconciliation
topics.content:
Virtual DOM

React creates an in-memory data structure cache (the Virtual DOM), computes the resulting differences, and then updates the browser's displayed DOM efficiently.

questions.text: What is the Virtual DOM in React?
options: A direct copy of the real DOM used for CSS styling
An in-memory representation of the real DOM
questions.correctAnswer: An in-memory representation of the real DOM
questions.explanation: React maintains a lightweight representation of the DOM in memory.

topics.title: Hooks in Depth
topics.content:
Common Hooks

Hooks let you use state and other React features without writing a class.

questions.text: How do you run a useEffect hook only once when the component mounts?
options: Pass an empty array [] as the second argument
Return a function from the effect
questions.correctAnswer: Pass an empty array [] as the second argument
questions.explanation: An empty dependency array tells React that your effect doesn’t depend on any values from props or state.

topics.title: React Suspense and Concurrent Mode
topics.content:
Suspense

<Suspense> lets your components 'wait' for something before they can render, showing a fallback UI while waiting.

questions.text: What is a primary benefit of React's concurrent rendering?
options: It reduces the JavaScript bundle size
It renders the UI faster by using multiple CPU threads
It allows React to pause rendering to handle high-priority events like user input
It completely eliminates the need for useEffect
questions.correctAnswer: It allows React to pause rendering to handle high-priority events like user input
questions.explanation: Concurrent rendering makes the rendering process interruptible, ensuring the UI remains responsive during heavy updates.

name: Node.js
description: An asynchronous event-driven JavaScript runtime designed to build scalable network applications.

topics.title: Event-Driven Architecture
topics.content:
Event Emitter

Node.js is heavily built around an event-driven architecture. The events module provides an EventEmitter class that triggers events and handles callbacks.

questions.text: Which core module in Node.js provides the EventEmitter class?
questions.correctAnswer: events
questions.explanation: The 'events' module exposes the EventEmitter class.

topics.title: Cluster Module and Worker Threads
topics.content:
Cluster vs Worker Threads

The cluster module allows you to create child processes that share server ports. worker_threads allow you to run JavaScript in parallel threads, useful for CPU-intensive tasks.

questions.text: When should you use worker_threads instead of the cluster module?
options: To handle more concurrent HTTP requests
questions.correctAnswer: To perform CPU-intensive JavaScript operations
questions.explanation: Worker threads are designed for running CPU-intensive operations (like cryptography or image processing) in parallel without blocking the main event loop.

name: Next.js
description: The React Framework for the Web, providing hybrid static & server rendering, and smart bundling.

topics.title: Server vs Client Components
topics.content:
App Router Architecture

In the Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default.

questions.text: How do you explicitly declare a Client Component in the Next.js App Router?
options: By using the 'use client' directive at the top of the file
By placing it in the /client directory
questions.correctAnswer: By using the 'use client' directive at the top of the file
questions.explanation: The 'use client' directive marks a file boundary where Next.js switches from Server to Client rendering.

topics.title: Server Actions and Mutations
topics.content:
Server Actions

Asynchronous functions that run on the server. They can be called directly from Client Components (via form actions or event handlers) to mutate data without needing to create API endpoints manually.

questions.text: What is a primary advantage of using Server Actions in Next.js?
options: They allow you to write CSS in JS
They eliminate the need to manually create API routes for data mutations
They run faster on the client side
questions.correctAnswer: They eliminate the need to manually create API routes for data mutations
questions.explanation: Server actions allow you to execute server-side code directly from client interactions without setting up intermediary API routes.

name: TypeScript
description: A strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript, giving you better tooling at any scale.

topics.title: Interfaces vs Types
topics.content:
Interfaces and Type Aliases

Both can be used to describe the shape of an object. Interfaces are better for public API definitions because they support declaration merging, whereas types can be used for unions, primitives, and mapped types.

questions.text: Which feature is unique to Interfaces and cannot be done with Type Aliases?
questions.correctAnswer: Declaration Merging
questions.explanation: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope will merge their declarations, which is highly useful for extending third-party libraries. Type aliases will throw an error.

topics.title: Generics
topics.content:
Understanding Generics

Generics allow you to create reusable components that can work over a variety of types rather than a single one.

questions.text: What does <T> typically represent in TypeScript?
questions.correctAnswer: A generic type parameter
questions.explanation: T is commonly used as a placeholder variable for a Generic Type.

topics.title: Utility Types & Mapped Types
topics.content:
Utility Types

TypeScript provides several utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record) to facilitate common type transformations.

Mapped Types

A mapped type is a generic type which uses a union of PropertyKeys (frequently created via a keyof) to iterate through keys to create a type.

questions.text: Which utility type constructs a type with all properties of T set to optional?
questions.correctAnswer: Partial<T>
questions.explanation: Partial<T> returns a type representing all subsets of a given type.

questions.text: What does the `keyof` operator do?
options: Returns the value of a key
Takes an object type and produces a string or numeric literal union of its keys
Checks if a key exists in an object at runtime
questions.correctAnswer: Takes an object type and produces a string or numeric literal union of its keys
questions.explanation: The keyof operator produces a union type of all public property names of a given type.

topics.title: Type Guards & Narrowing
topics.content:
Narrowing

TypeScript can narrow types down to more specific types using type guards like typeof, instanceof, or custom type predicate functions returning arg is Type.

questions.text: How do you define a custom type guard in TypeScript?
options: By using the `is` keyword in the return type (e.g., `animal is Fish`)
By throwing an Error on type mismatch
questions.correctAnswer: By using the `is` keyword in the return type (e.g., `animal is Fish`)
questions.explanation: A custom type guard function must return a type predicate in the form `parameterName is Type`.

name: MongoDB
description: A document-based, NoSQL database program that uses JSON-like documents with optional schemas.

topics.title: NoSQL Concepts & Documents
topics.content:
Document Model

MongoDB stores data in flexible, JSON-like documents. This means fields can vary from document to document and data structure can be changed over time.

questions.text: In MongoDB, a single record is called a:
questions.correctAnswer: Document
questions.explanation: In MongoDB, data is stored in BSON Documents (binary JSON), analogous to rows in a relational database.

topics.title: Aggregation Framework
topics.content:
Aggregations

The aggregation pipeline is a framework for data aggregation modeled on the concept of data processing pipelines. Documents enter a multi-stage pipeline that transforms the documents into aggregated results.

questions.text: Which aggregation stage is used to filter documents?
questions.correctAnswer: $match
questions.explanation: $match filters the documents to pass only the documents that match the specified condition(s) to the next pipeline stage.

topics.title: Indexing & Performance
topics.content:
Indexes

Indexes support the efficient execution of queries in MongoDB. Without indexes, MongoDB must perform a collection scan, i.e. scan every document in a collection, to select those documents that match the query statement.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about Compound Indexes?
options: They can only contain two fields
The order of fields in the index does not matter
The order of fields matters due to the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) rule
They are created automatically for every collection
questions.correctAnswer: The order of fields matters due to the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) rule
questions.explanation: In compound indexes, field order is crucial. The ESR rule is a guideline for ordering fields: Equality first, then Sort, then Range.

topics.title: Replication & Sharding
topics.content:
Scaling MongoDB

Replication (Replica Sets): Provides redundancy and high availability.
Sharding: Distributes data across multiple machines (Horizontal scaling).

questions.text: In a MongoDB Replica Set, what happens if the Primary node goes down?
options: The database becomes completely inaccessible forever
An election is held among the Secondary nodes to choose a new Primary
A Secondary node is randomly assigned without an election
questions.correctAnswer: An election is held among the Secondary nodes to choose a new Primary
questions.explanation: Replica sets provide automatic failover through an election process.

name: System Design
description: The process of defining the architecture, modules, interfaces, and data for a system to satisfy specified requirements.

topics.title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal
topics.content:
Scaling Methods

Vertical Scaling (Scale-Up): Adding more power (CPU, RAM) to your existing machine.
Horizontal Scaling (Scale-Out): Adding more machines to your pool of resources.

questions.text: What is a primary disadvantage of Vertical Scaling?
options: It has a hard hardware limit and creates a single point of failure
Data consistency is difficult to maintain
questions.correctAnswer: It has a hard hardware limit and creates a single point of failure
questions.explanation: You can only add so much RAM or CPU to one machine, and if that machine goes down, the entire system is down.

topics.title: Caching Strategies
topics.content:
Caching

Caching stores copies of frequently accessed data in a temporary, fast-access storage layer (like Redis or Memcached). Strategies include Cache-Aside, Read-Through, and Write-Through.

questions.text: In the Cache-Aside pattern, what happens when a cache miss occurs?
options: The cache automatically fetches data from the DB
The application queries the DB, returns the data, and writes it to the cache
The database writes it to the cache directly
questions.correctAnswer: The application queries the DB, returns the data, and writes it to the cache
questions.explanation: In Cache-Aside, the application code is responsible for checking the cache, querying the database on a miss, and then updating the cache.

topics.title: Message Queues & Event-Driven Architecture
topics.content:
Asynchronous Processing

Message queues (like RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) are used to decouple heavy processing, to buffer or batch work, and to smooth spiky workloads.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes Apache Kafka?
questions.correctAnswer: A distributed event streaming platform
questions.explanation: Kafka is optimized for high-throughput, low-latency event streaming and log aggregation.

topics.title: CAP Theorem
topics.content:
The CAP Theorem

States that it is impossible for a distributed data store to simultaneously provide more than two out of the following three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.

questions.text: In the context of the CAP Theorem, what does Partition Tolerance mean?
options: The system can be divided into smaller tables
The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped/delayed by the network
The data is partitioned equally across disks
Every read receives the most recent write
questions.correctAnswer: The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped/delayed by the network
questions.explanation: Partition tolerance implies the system functions even if network partitions occur.

questions.text: Which combination does a typical relational database (like PostgreSQL) prioritize?
questions.correctAnswer: CA (Consistency & Availability)
questions.explanation: Traditional RDBMS prioritize Consistency and Availability, but generally fail under network partitions (they are not typically distributed by default).

name: Python
description: An interpreted, high-level, general-purpose programming language.

topics.title: Lists vs Tuples
topics.content:
Data Structures

Lists are mutable sequences, meaning their elements can be changed after creation. Tuples are immutable sequences.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about Tuples in Python?
options: They are declared using square brackets []
questions.correctAnswer: They are immutable
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be modified after they are created.

topics.title: Decorators
topics.content:
Decorators

A decorator is a design pattern in Python that allows a user to add new functionality to an existing object without modifying its structure.

questions.text: Which symbol is used to apply a decorator in Python?
questions.explanation: The @ symbol is syntactic sugar for passing a function into another function (the decorator).

name: SQL
description: Structured Query Language for storing, manipulating and retrieving data in databases.

topics.title: JOINs
topics.content:
SQL JOINs

A JOIN clause is used to combine rows from two or more tables, based on a related column between them.

questions.text: Which JOIN returns all records when there is a match in either left or right table?
questions.correctAnswer: FULL OUTER JOIN
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all matching records from both tables whether the other table matches or not.
